parties:
Polish Ocean Lines, and another’s ------ Appellants.
VS
Al-Amin Seatrans Ltd. and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
12. In support of his contention that the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation Mr. Muhammad Ohiullah cited Article 3 Rule 6 of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 which is incorporated in the Bill of Lading and he further cited the decisions of 14 BLC (AD) 115, 61 DLR 463, 13 BLC 763, 1983 BLD 3, 10 DLR 307, 59 DLR 151, 12 DLR 418, 13 DLR 186, AIR 1937 Sind 11 and AIR 1932 Bombay 330 wherein it has been clearly laid down that unless a suit is brought against the carrier within 1 year from the date of discharge of the cargo the suit is barred by limitation. We find that in the instant case the vessel MV Grunwald came to Bangladesh on 12th March, 1986 and completed discharge of her cargo on 27th March, 1986. Thereafter as per the allegation of the plaintiff the Chittagong Port Authority on 12th February, 1991 issued a shortlanding certificate (although the same was neither filed in the suit nor exhibited) and the Assistant Collector of Customs issued a penalty order imposing a penalty of Taka 21,64,901 vide order No.22 on the plaintiff/ Respondent No. 1 on 16th March, 1991 and the adjudication order passed by the Assistant Commissioner of Customs along with the penalty bill was sent by the plaintiff/respondent No. 1 to the Appellant/ defendant Nos.1 and 2 on 18-3-1991. We fail to understand how the Court below could have decreed the suit against the Appellants/ Defendant No. 1 and 2 despite the fact that the plaintiff/respondent No. 1 itself had given the declaration under section 55(e) of the Customs Act, 1969 making itself answerable for any kinds of shortage that may be found during the discharge of the cargo from the vessel MV Grunwald. We also find it difficult to understand how the trial Court could have decreed the suit despite the fact that a period of almost 5 years had elapsed since the cargo had been discharged from the vessel MV Grunwald although the suit was filed long beyond the prescribed period of limitation. It is pertinent to note that even though the plaintiff/respondent No. 1 had filed this money suit claiming to recover customs penalty from the protecting agent of the owners of the vessel the suit is clearly not maintainable because the Government of Bangladesh/Customs Authorities had never assigned its rights to the plaintiff/Respondent No. 1 and the plaintiff respondent No. 1 had also never acquired any right through the Government of Bangladesh to file the suit to recover such customs dues and penalty from the Appellants/ Defendant Nos. 1 and 2. It was solely within the domain and discretion of the Customs Authorities to commence any action against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2/ Appellants to recover any customs dues and not for the plaintiff to take the same on its own shoulders when the plaintiff clearly had no authority to file such suit. 

 13. Finally, Mr Muhammad Ohiullah the learned Advocate for the Appellants submitted that the plaintiff attached the vessel MV Grunwald under Order XXXVIII Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure when the vessel came to Chittagong during her subsequent voyage and the Defendant Nos. 1 and 2/Appellants were into coerced into giving a Bank Guarantee to release the vessel from the order of attachment passed by the Court below. He submitted that the very attachment of the vessel MV Grunwald under Order XXXVIII Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure was prima facie illegal. In support of his contentions he referred to the cases of 28 DLR 231, 31 DLR (AD) 114, 45 DLR 591 and 17 BID 159. We find force in such contention of Mr Muhammad Ohiullah. In such view of the matter we also hold that the attachment of the vessel MV Grunwald under Order XXXVIII Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure was also clearly illegal.
